content: The health and welfare of populations must be prioritized, ensuring the resilience and self-reliance of health systems. This is essential to minimize health hazards and vulnerabilities while enabling effective responses and recovery during emergencies and disasters. The tragic loss of life, injuries, diseases, and disabilities resulting from such crises is deeply regrettable. Emergencies and disasters often lead to the destruction of hospitals and health infrastructure, weakening the ability of health systems to deliver services and hindering progress in health development and the achievement of global health goals. The increasing risks posed by poverty, urbanization, and climate change are expected to exacerbate the health impacts of emergencies and disasters on many countries and communities. Most actions to manage health risks from natural, biological, technological, and societal hazards, including emergency responses, are carried out by local and national actors across various health disciplines. These include mass casualty management, mental health, noncommunicable and communicable diseases, environmental health, maternal and newborn health, reproductive health, nutrition, and other cross-cutting health issues. The contributions of other sectors, such as local governments, planners, architects, engineers, emergency services, civil protection, and academia, are critical to the health and well-being of populations at risk from emergencies and disasters. However, the capacity of countries and communities to manage major emergencies is often overwhelmed, with coordination, communication, and logistics frequently identified as the weakest aspects of health emergency management. Palliative care and symptom relief should be integrated into responses to humanitarian emergencies and crises. Some countries, including those with low-income or emerging economies, have successfully reduced mortality and morbidity in disaster situations through investments in emergency and disaster risk-reduction measures, supported by local, regional, and global partners. The World Health Organization (WHO) plays a vital role as part of the International Strategy for Disaster Reduction system and as the health cluster lead within the humanitarian reform framework. WHO collaborates closely with international entities such as the United Nations, UNICEF, the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, and other nongovernmental organizations to support country capacity development and institutional strengthening for multisectoral emergency and disaster risk management, including disaster risk reduction. Building on international campaigns and initiatives, such as the World Disaster Reduction Campaigns and World Health Day themes, actions have been taken at local, national, and global levels to reduce health risks from emergencies and disasters. Improved health outcomes from such crises require urgent additional actions at all levels to ensure timely and effective health risk reduction and response measures. Health services must remain operational during emergencies when they are most needed, considering the differential impacts of disasters on men and women. Member States are urged to strengthen all-hazards health emergency and disaster risk management programs, including disaster risk reduction, preparedness, and response, as part of national and subnational health systems. These programs should be supported by effective legislation, regulations, and enforcement measures to improve health outcomes, reduce mortality and morbidity, protect health infrastructure, and enhance the resilience of health systems and society. A gender perspective should be integrated into all phases of these programs. Countries should integrate health emergency and disaster risk management programs into national health plans and institutionalize capacities for coordinated health and multisectoral actions. This includes assessing risks, proactively reducing risks, and preparing for, responding to, and recovering from emergencies and disasters. Governments and agencies should have access to information on hazardous materials to support effective health emergency and disaster risk management. Programs should be developed to ensure hospitals and health facilities are safe and prepared for emergencies. This includes locating and constructing new facilities to withstand local hazards, assessing the safety of existing facilities, and taking remedial actions. All health facilities should be prepared to respond to internal and external emergencies. Regional and subregional collaboration, as well as interregional cooperation within WHO, should be promoted to share experiences and expertise for capacity development in risk reduction, response, and recovery. The role of the local health workforce in health emergency management systems should be strengthened through enhanced planning, training, and access to resources. Member States, donors, and development partners are called upon to allocate sufficient resources for health emergency and disaster risk management programs through international cooperation, humanitarian appeals, and support for WHO’s role in these matters. The WHO Director-General is requested to ensure that WHO has enhanced capacity and resources at all levels to provide technical guidance and support to Member States for developing health emergency and disaster risk management programs. Collaboration with relevant entities in public, private, nongovernmental, and academic sectors should be strengthened to support country and community health emergency management efforts. The evidence base for health emergency and disaster risk management, including operational research and economic assessments, should be strengthened. National and subnational assessments of risks and capacities should be supported to catalyze action and strengthen health emergency management capacities. The international transportation of humanitarian supplies containing narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances is often hindered by regulatory requirements for import and export authorizations. This results in delays that deprive disaster-stricken populations of adequate pain relief and sedation, causing additional human suffering. A practical solution is urgently needed to address this issue. The International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) has recommended limiting control obligations to exporting countries' authorities in emergency situations. This principle has been endorsed by the United Nations and WHO, which have developed model guidelines to simplify regulatory procedures for the international provision of controlled medicines during emergencies. These guidelines aim to balance the timely provision of essential medicines with minimizing the risk of diversion.
